title: Strings and drums
hookLine: the old kirtan used string instruments and the pakhawaj drum

cards: A carved wooden body, a skin stretched over its belly, strings running down its neck.
In the stories of Guru Nanak's travels, an instrument like that walks the roads beside him: the rabab, in the hands of his companion, Bhai Mardana.
In the janamsakhis, the Guru asks Mardana to play, and the hymn comes once the music has begun. So in Sikh memory, kirtan starts with a string being touched.

teach.b: The phrase is tanti saaj. Saaj is an instrument; tanti, of strings. It's how Sikh musicians name the family of string instruments the older kirtan was played on.
Tradition names others: the saranda, played with a bow; the taus, its body carved like a peacock; the dilruba, a lighter cousin of the taus.
Under them sat a drum, the pakhawaj, long and barrel-shaped, played with the hands on both ends. Strings and skin: one carries the melody, the other keeps the beat. Why would that matter to a raga?

teach.h: A STRING CAN SLIDE BETWEEN NOTES.
teach.b: Because a raga lives partly in the spaces between its notes, the slides and bends from one to the next. A string can slide. A bow can hold a note and lean into it.
Today the harmonium and the tabla are a familiar sound in gurdwaras, and they carry much of the kirtan heard there.
Alongside them, some musicians and teachers have worked to bring the older strings back, so the ragas can be heard with those slides again, and gurdwaras and kirtan schools make room for both.
The Granth itself hears music at the holiest door.

In the Japji, in the pauri that asks what the Creator's gate is like, Guru Nanak lists the sounds there: instruments beyond counting, and players beyond counting, all singing. The whole creation is the band.
And this week has moved the same way, from the hard century and the year three close to raag, to ghar and rahao, to the instruments themselves.

how: Kirtan in gurdwaras today is heard with harmonium and tabla, and some ragis and kirtan schools also teach and perform on the older string instruments, the rabab, saranda, taus and dilruba, with the pakhawaj drum.

games.q: you want a raga's slides between notes to be heard. which instrument keeps them best?
games.why: a string can slide from note to note and a bow can lean into a note, so the spaces where a raga lives can be heard.

practice: Play a recording of kirtan, or any music with strings in it, and follow only the string, listening for the slide where a key would jump and a string can glide; then listen underneath for the drum keeping time.
With no recording near you, pluck a rubber band or a taut thread and listen until the sound is gone. If you pray, let Waheguru sound inside, as quietly as the end of a plucked note.

wordCard.voice: Tanti saaj. String instruments: the rabab, the saranda, the taus, the dilruba, the older voices of kirtan, with the pakhawaj drum beneath them. Today's word.
